<reason>Both sides argued competently and the debate stayed genuinely on the motion. PRO built a consistent, clean distinction between legitimate tenancy screening and a categorical income-source veto, conceded real administrative burdens but insisted they must be assessed case-by-case rather than presumed, and answered CON's pressure questions with proper A1/A2 structure. CON's strongest contribution was concrete mechanism work (bundled third-party contract, rent caps, inspection timing) and a genuinely original closing move: the "mandate can subtract supply permanently, incentives can only fail to add it" asymmetry. That framing is rhetorically sharp, but it has a live gap PRO exposed in closing — it treats continued exclusion under an incentives-only regime as costless, when that is exactly the certain, ongoing harm the mandate targets, versus CON's speculative and unquantified exit risk (which CON itself conceded was unquantified in B4.5). CON's final reply to that charge (B5.2) reasserts "direction over magnitude" without actually rebutting the "costless exclusion" point, so PRO's rebuttal stands largely undamaged at the close. CON's opening was also flagged as clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost per the judging frame. On balance PRO's case is slightly more complete and better defended through the final exchange, giving it a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange is CON's asymmetry argument (B4.3/B5.1) against PRO's closing counter that this framing "treats continued exclusion as costless" (A5.3); CON's final reply reasserts the asymmetry but never actually answers that specific charge, leaving PRO's rebuttal live at the end of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
